t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The aim of this session is to isolate acidic, neutral and weakly basic poisons by the acidified water method and to explain the theoretical basis of the method. The plan consists of three items. The first: isolation of acidic, neutral and weakly basic substances with the help of acidified water. The second: extraction of the isolate with an organic solvent under acidic and alkaline conditions, dividing the poison into two groups. The third: testing the aqueous isolate for pachycarpine.

There are four expected outcomes of the session. First, you will learn the method of isolating acidic, neutral and weakly basic substances from physical evidence with acidified water. Second, from the isolate obtained, by extraction with chloroform under acidic and alkaline conditions, you will divide the "organic poisons" into two groups. Third, you will compare general and specific methods of isolation and learn to choose a method according to the object and the properties of the substance. Fourth, you will master purifying the substances isolated under acidic conditions from "foreign" substances.

t: Session map: isolation with polar solvents
n: This is the session map. The isolate is extracted under acidic and alkaline conditions and divided into two groups. The main methods of isolation with polar solvents: Stas–Otto, that is, acidified alcohol, and the methods of A. A. Vasilyeva and V. F. Kramarenko, that is, acidified water. In the Stas–Otto method, ethyl alcohol with oxalic acid is used. In the Vasilyeva method, water with oxalic acid and extraction with chloroform are used. In the Kramarenko method, water with sulphuric acid and centrifugation are used. At the end, an acidic and an alkaline isolate are obtained, and pachycarpine is tested for the iodide ion.

First we look at the origin of the alcohol and water methods. The acidified alcohol method was proposed in about the 1840s. Stas in 1851 relied on the good solubility of alkaloid salts in alcohol, and Otto in 1856 used alcohol with oxalic or tartaric acid. In this method an emulsion hardly forms. The acidified water method was applied in 1861 by Uslar and Erdmann, who proposed acidifying the object with hydrochloric acid. Later authors recommended phosphoric acid, sulphuric acid and other mineral and organic acids. The water method is a rapid method.

In the Dragendorff method, the object is acidified with sulphuric acid and the aqueous solution is evaporated to a syrup. The syrup is infused with 96% alcohol for 24 hours and filtered. The filtrate is mixed with water and extracted with petrol, petroleum ether and chloroform. Then it is made alkaline with ammonia and extracted with petrol and isoamyl alcohol, the extracts are combined and tested for alkaloids. The disadvantage of this method is that heating and evaporating the sulphuric acid extract hydrolyses most alkaloids of the ester type and gives a dirty residue.

In his method, Kramarenko recommended taking into account the pH of the object, the nature of the organic solvents and the effect of electrolytes. At pH 2.5–3 the complex is broken down. In choosing the solvent, ether is used at the acidic stage and chloroform at the alkaline stage. As the electrolyte, the isolate is saturated with (NH4)2SO4. Instead of filtration, centrifugation is used. All this is connected with the fact that alkaloids in the body may change under the action of hydrolysis, oxidation, reduction and binding to proteins.

Now pay attention to alkaloid–protein complexes. Alkaloids bind well to proteins in a weakly acidic medium, at pH 4–5, and this property strengthens as pH increases. In a living body the pH is 7.3–7.5, while in a corpse it is about 6.2, so alkaloids are mainly found in the bound state. To break down the complexes, the pH of the medium must be changed. At pH 2.5–3 this is achieved. Remember: the complex must be broken down before isolation.

This slide gives the scheme of the reaction between an alkaloid and a protein. Alkaloids, combining with protein substances, can form complexes that are insoluble in water. This process occurs in a weakly acidic medium, at pH 4–5, and as pH increases the ability of alkaloids to bind to protein strengthens. Therefore, in isolating alkaloids, the pH is changed in order to break down the complexes: for breaking down, the pH is brought to 2.5–3. That is, the pH of the medium determines the success of the isolation.

Before starting the work we prepare the equipment. Necessary items: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual materials; the work takes place in a specially equipped laboratory room. First the external appearance of the object under test is determined: colour, smell, foreign substances, preservatives and mass. This information is recorded in the workbook. Then the pH of the object is determined using universal indicator and an ion meter.

t: Origin of the acidified water methods
n: We look at the history of the acidified water methods. In 1942, Stepanov and Shvaykova developed the method of water acidified with oxalic acid. In 1946, Vasilyeva applied this method to isolate alkaloids from a corpse organ, which is why the method is called the Shvaykova–Vasilyeva method. In 1956–1961, Kramarenko improved the method: the pH of the medium, the nature of the solvent and the effect of electrolytes were taken into account, and centrifugation was introduced instead of filtration. Before that, Stas in 1851 proposed the acidified alcohol method, Otto supplemented it in 1856, and Uslar and Erdmann applied the acidified water method in 1861.

The start of the Vasilyeva method. First 100 g of the object is minced and mixed with water. The ratio is 1:2 for a biological object and 1:12 for a plant object. Then the pH is brought to 2.0–2.5 with oxalic acid solution. The mixture is infused for two hours and shaken from time to time during this. After that the isolate is ready for the next stage of extraction.

Remember the key values of the Vasilyeva method. Amount of object 100 g; water ratio 1:2 for a biological object and 1:12 for plant objects. The acidic medium pH 2.0–2.5 is established with oxalic acid. Infusion lasts two hours. At the acidic and alkaline stages, 3 times 10 ml of chloroform is used each time. At the alkaline stage the pH is brought to 8.0–9.0 with 25% ammonium hydroxide.

In the acidic extraction stage, the isolate strained through gauze is shaken 3 times with 10 ml of chloroform, 5 minutes each time. The chloroform solution is passed through a double filter into a dry glass vessel. From this isolate, testing for acidic, neutral and weakly basic substances is carried out. That is, the first chloroform extract contains precisely this group of substances.

Alkaline extraction. The aqueous part left after the acidic extraction is brought to pH 8.0–9.0 with 25% ammonium hydroxide. Then it is shaken 3 times with 10 ml of chloroform. The chloroform portions are combined and filtered into a dry vessel. From this isolate, testing for bases and weak bases is carried out. Thus the second extract gives poisons with basic properties.

The stage of drying and assessing the extracts. The acidic and alkaline chloroform extracts are evaporated at room temperature. The colour, smell and consistency of the residue are determined. If necessary, the residue is purified from foreign substances and testing for individual substances is continued. Remember: evaporation is carried out at room temperature, so the substances are not destroyed.

Now the start of the Kramarenko method. 100 g of the object is placed in a 250–500 ml beaker and covered with 0.02 M sulphuric acid. The pH is checked with universal indicator. If the pH is below 2.5, it is brought to 2.5 with 20% sulphuric acid. Then the mixture is stirred from time to time, left for two hours and strained through gauze.

The key values of the Kramarenko method. Object 100 g, sulphuric acid 0.02 M, first pH 2.5. If the pH is below 2.5, it is brought to 2.5 with 20% H2SO4. The first infusion lasts 2 hours, the second 1 hour; the centrifuge tube is 200 ml. At the acidic stage, extraction with ether 2 x 40 ml is carried out. At the alkaline stage the pH is brought to 8.0–9.0 with 20% NaOH and chloroform is used 3 times.

We compare the methods. In the Stas–Otto method, ethyl alcohol with oxalic acid is used, the object is infused for 1 day, and the alcoholic solutions are evaporated at 35 °C. In the Vasilyeva method, water with oxalic acid is used, pH 2.0–2.5, infusion for two hours, chloroform 3 x 10 ml. In the Kramarenko method, pH 2.5 is established with 0.02 M sulphuric acid, the mixture is centrifuged, saturated with ammonium sulphate, then extracted with ether 2 x 40 ml and chloroform.

t: Methods of purification from foreign substances
n: The methods of purification from foreign substances differ in each procedure. In the Stas–Otto method, the alcoholic syrup is precipitated with 96% ethyl alcohol from foreign and protein substances, then purified with ether, that is, three purifications with ether are carried out. In the Vasilyeva method, the isolate is strained through gauze and the chloroform extract is passed through a double filter. In the Kramarenko method, saturation with ammonium sulphate, centrifugation and extraction with ether 2 x 40 ml are used.

Table of times and volumes. In the Vasilyeva method, the first infusion is 2 hours, chloroform 3 x 10 ml, shaking 5 minutes each time. In the Kramarenko method, the first infusion is 2 hours, the second one hour, the precipitate is treated with 20–30 ml of acid for 2 hours, ether 2 x 40 ml. After saturation with ammonium sulphate, the precipitate is separated by centrifugation after 1–2 hours. Study these figures by comparing them.

t: Kramarenko method: second infusion and centrifuge
n: The stage of second infusion and centrifuge in the Kramarenko method. The solid part is infused a second time for one hour with 0.02 M sulphuric acid at pH 2.5. The sulphuric acid solutions are combined and centrifuged in a 200 ml centrifuge tube. The precipitate is infused with 20–30 ml of 0.02 M sulphuric acid for two hours and centrifuged again. The aqueous layer is added to the general isolate.

The stage of removing protein. To purify from proteins and foreign substances, the isolate is slowly saturated with ammonium sulphate salt. After one or two hours, the precipitate that has formed is separated by centrifugation. The pH of the aqueous layer is checked and brought to pH 2.0–2.5 with 10% sulphuric acid. After that the isolate is ready for extraction with 2 x 40 ml of ethyl ether.

Acidic extraction. The acidic aqueous layer is extracted twice with 40 ml of ethyl ether. In the ether extract, testing for poisonous substances extracted under acidic conditions is carried out. But the ether extract may also be discarded for another purpose, that is, to obtain foreign substances. Remember: the main alkaline stage continues with the aqueous layer.

The alkaline extraction stage. The aqueous layer is brought to pH 8.0–9.0 with 20% sodium hydroxide. Then it is extracted three times with chloroform, and the volume of chloroform should be 1/3 of the volume of the aqueous layer. The chloroform extracts are combined and evaporated on a water bath until 10–15 ml remains, and the rest at room temperature. The dry residue is dissolved in 10 ml of 0.1 M hydrochloric acid and tested for poisons with basic properties.

Why precisely NaOH is used? When 20% sodium hydroxide is added to the acidic aqueous solution, the pH of the medium changes owing to the ammonia released. Reaction: (NH4)2SO4 + 2NaOH → 2NH4OH + Na2SO4. That is, ammonium sulphate is converted by the alkali into ammonium hydroxide and sodium sulphate. After that the aqueous layer is extracted with chloroform 3 times.

Now the iodide ion reaction for pachycarpine. The aqueous part left after the alkaline extraction is acidified with sulphuric acid to an acidic medium. If sodium nitrite and chloroform are added and shaken, in the presence of the iodide ion the chloroform layer turns red-pink, that is, red-violet. Reaction: 2NH4I + 2NaNO2 + 2H2SO4 → I2 + Na2SO4 + (NH4)2SO4 + 2NO + 2H2O. The colour is given by I2 in chloroform.

The evaporation regimes differ according to the methods. In the Stas–Otto method, alcoholic solutions are evaporated at a temperature of 35 °C until a small amount of alcohol remains. In the Vasilyeva method, the acidic and alkaline chloroform extracts are evaporated at room temperature. In the Kramarenko method, the chloroform extracts are evaporated on a water bath until 10–15 ml remains, and the rest is evaporated at room temperature.

Testing for pachycarpine, that is, the test for the iodide ion. In both methods, the last aqueous residue is tested for the iodide ion for pachycarpine. For this, sulphuric acid, 1–2 drops of NaNO2 and 1 ml of chloroform are added to 5 ml of the aqueous part and shaken. The chloroform layer may become red-violet. Task: explain for what reason this colour forms.

We compare the two methods. In the Vasilyeva method the acid is oxalic, acidic pH 2.0–2.5, at the alkaline stage 25% NH4OH with pH 8.0–9.0, and the solvent of the acidic stage is 3 x 10 ml of chloroform. In the Kramarenko method the acid is 0.02 M H2SO4, acidic pH 2.5, at the alkaline stage 20% NaOH with pH 8.0–9.0, and the solvent of the acidic stage is 2 x 40 ml of ether. The Vasilyeva method is performed quickly and does not require expensive reagents. In the Kramarenko method, centrifugation instead of filtration, pH 2.5 and purification from protein with ammonium sulphate are used.

t: Disadvantage and advantage of the method (lecture)
n: Advantages and disadvantages of the methods. The Vasilyeva method is performed quickly and without expensive reagents, but substances insoluble in acidified water are difficult to isolate. Toxicological substances cannot be completely isolated from a putrefied object, because a stable emulsion forms during extraction. The Kramarenko method, on the other hand, is sensitive, poisonous substances are isolated completely, it is performed relatively quickly and the reagents are easy to find. These differences are decisive in choosing the method.

Poisons are divided into two groups, and each isolate is analysed separately. In the acidic isolate, barbiturates, the neutral substance phenacetin, organic acids, that is, salicylic and picric acid, and weakly basic alkaloids, for example caffeine and strychnine, are tested. In the alkaline isolate, alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are tested. That is, the first isolate gives acidic, neutral and weakly basic substances, the second gives basic substances.

Substances isolated with polar solvents. With acidified water and alcohol, mainly drug substances in the crystalline state are isolated. In a full analysis, the expert chemist tests for 28 substances from this group: 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. The series of barbiturates includes barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal sodium, cyclobarbital, hexobarbital and benzonal. Among the alkaloids are morphine, codeine, dionine, heroin, papaverine, strychnine, atropine, cocaine, pachycarpine, nicotine and quinine. They may have acidic, basic and neutral properties, so they are extracted from aqueous solution with organic solvents.

Liquid alkaloids have their own features of isolation. They include anabasine, nicotine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecoline. In base form they are oily, fairly volatile liquids with a characteristic smell, readily soluble in organic solvents. In salt form they dissolve well in water. Therefore they are distilled from the biological object with steam under alkaline conditions, the distillate is brought to an alkaline medium and extracted with chloroform.

t: Cadaveric alkaloids and choice of method
n: Cadaveric alkaloids and the choice of method. In methods with polar solvents, a stable emulsion may form from a putrefied object, whereas in the Stas–Otto method there is hardly any emulsion. The method is chosen according to the nature of the object and the physicochemical properties of the poisonous substance. At present, on the basis of the Stas–Otto, Vasilyeva and Kramarenko methods, isolation is carried out at pH 2.5–3.0, and alkaloids are extracted from the aqueous isolate at pH 9.

Group work assignment. Group 1 presents the Stas–Otto method, its essence, advantages and disadvantages. Group 2 sets out the method of A. A. Vasilyeva, its essence, advantages and disadvantages. Group 3 explains the method of V. F. Kramarenko, its essence, advantages and disadvantages. The groups fill in a K/W/L table: what I know, what I want to know, what I have learned.

The Stas–Otto method, that is, the acidified alcohol method. The method was proposed in 1851 by the Belgian J. S. Stas on the basis of the good solubility of alkaloids in salt form in alcohol. In 1856, F. Otto proposed purifying the alcoholic extract, which is why the method is called the Stas–Otto method. Disadvantages: it takes a long time, has low sensitivity, needs costly alcohol, and results are variable. Advantage: substances can be isolated from a putrefied object, because purification is carried out in alcohol and an emulsion hardly forms.

Situational problems. The first problem: Boboyor S., born in 1976, whose corpse was found; the corpse has begun to putrefy. State which method is used to isolate the poisonous substance and characterise the method. The second problem: Berdiyorov V., born in 1980, whose corpse has been delivered. Apply the method for complete and pure isolation of the alkaloid from the object. Blitz task: choose correctly the sequence of extraction stages in the Stas–Otto and Kramarenko methods.

Review questions. First: which methods are used in isolating acidic, neutral and weakly basic substances from a biological object. Second: which substances pass into the chloroform layer in an acidic medium and why. Third: at which stages, in isolating substances with water acidified with sulphuric acid, is purification from foreign substances carried out. Fourth: what is done with the aqueous layer in the acidified water method after the chloroform layer has been separated.

We conclude. The acidified water method, that is, the Vasilyeva and Kramarenko methods, isolates acidic, neutral and weakly basic poisons. The isolate is extracted under acidic and alkaline conditions and divided into two groups, and the aqueous residue is tested for pachycarpine. The isolate of each group is analysed separately and, if necessary, purified from foreign substances.
